title: Atoms, shells and valence electrons
summary: Atomic number, electron shells, why silicon has four valence electrons and forms four bonds, and why boron and phosphorus are the dopants. Needed for week 2.

diagrams.title: Electron shells of the elements that matter for silicon
diagrams.tryThis: Compare Si with P and B: count the outer-shell electrons and see what each atom does when it replaces a Si atom in the crystal.

checks.prompt: Arsenic has atomic number 33: shells hold 2, 8, 18 and then the rest. How many valence electrons does As have?
hints: Valence electrons are the ones in the outermost, unfilled shell.
solution: Outer shell: 33 − 28 = **5** valence electrons, like phosphorus. So As is a donor in silicon (book ex. 6.6).

checks.prompt: A simple cubic cell has one atom on each of its 8 corners and nothing else. How many atoms belong to one cell?

errors.feedback: Each corner atom is shared by the 8 cubes that meet there, so only 1/8 of it belongs to this cell.

hints: Neighbouring cells share atoms on corners and faces.
A corner is shared by 8 cubes, a face by 2.
solution: Every corner atom is shared by 8 cubes, so it counts for 1/8.
8 × 1/8 = **1** atom per cell. (The diamond cell of silicon adds 6 face atoms × ½ and 4 inside: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.)

checks.prompt: A phosphorus atom (atomic number 15) replaces a silicon atom (14). What is the net charge added to the crystal?

options.text: Zero: P has one electron more but also one proton more.
options.feedback: Right: a neutral atom replaces a neutral atom. Only when the fifth electron leaves does the P atom become a fixed positive ion, balanced by that free electron.
The extra electron comes with an extra proton in the nucleus. Count both.
P is only an ion after donating its electron, and then the free electron balances it.
The other four valence electrons replace silicon's four; and all are balanced by protons.

hints: An atom with atomic number Z has Z protons and, if neutral, Z electrons.
Compare the number of protons and electrons of P with those of Si.
solution: P: 15 protons, 15 electrons. Si: 14 and 14. Swapping them adds one proton **and** one electron: net charge zero (instruction 2 Q2c).
